title: AfterQuery reportedly becomes Y Combinator’s fastest-ever unicorn, now valued at $3.2B
content:
AI training-data startup AfterQuery has reportedly raised a round that valued it at $3.2 billion. This just five months after announcing its $30 million Series A at a $300 million valuation in April.
That’s more than a 10x increase in less than half a year and, according to Y Combinator partner Gustaf Alströmer, the fastest that any startup has gone from launch to unicorn status in the accelerator’s history. AfterQuery’s founders, today 22 and 23 years old, attended Y Combinator’s Winter 2025 cohort, just 18 months ago.
In April, the San Francisco startup said it had reached an annualized revenue run rate of $100 million and that it was working with many of the biggest labs. It has named companies including Nvidia, Legora and the Korean AI lab Motif Technologies, as customers.
AfterQuery is among the new crop of startups following in the footsteps of Mercor and Scale that employ knowledge professionals like doctors, lawyers, and other specialists, to do model training. However, rather than ensuring that models answer questions accurately, AfterQuery trains models and agents on how to work like professionals would to complete tasks — what the company describes as “encoding the patterns, decisions, and reasoning of the world’s best practitioners.”
Forbes first reported on the round. AfterQuery could not be immediately reached for comment.

report.summary: AI training-data startup AfterQuery hits $3.2B valuation five months after Series A, becoming Y Combinator's fastest unicorn.
report.background: AfterQuery is part of a new wave of AI infrastructure startups that don't build models themselves but supply the premium human expertise needed to train and fine-tune them. The San Francisco company, founded by two young entrepreneurs who went through Y Combinator's Winter 2025 cohort just 18 months ago, specializes in using professionals like doctors, lawyers, and other specialists to teach AI systems how to complete real-world tasks — not just answer questions. In April, the startup reported $100 million in annualized revenue and named Nvidia, Legora, and Korean AI lab Motif Technologies as customers. Now, according to Forbes, AfterQuery has raised a round valuing it at $3.2 billion, a tenfold jump from its April valuation. The company sits alongside data-labeling rivals Mercor and Scale AI, but differentiates itself by focusing on encoding the decision-making patterns of top practitioners rather than simple factual accuracy.
key_points: AfterQuery went from a $300 million valuation in April to a $3.2 billion valuation in September — a 10x increase in under five months. Y Combinator partner Gustaf Alströmer called it the fastest launch-to-unicorn journey in the accelerator's history, underscoring intense investor appetite for AI training-data startups.

The company claims an annualized revenue run rate of $100 million, a remarkable figure for a startup that emerged from YC only 18 months ago. Its customer roster includes major AI players like Nvidia, Legora, and Korea's Motif Technologies, showing that top labs are willing to pay heavily for expert-guided training data.

AfterQuery's approach involves hiring knowledge professionals — doctors, lawyers, and other specialists — to train AI agents on how to work like professionals. Instead of ensuring models give correct answers, AfterQuery says it encodes the patterns, decisions, and reasoning of the world's best practitioners, making AI useful for complex, multi-step professional tasks.

The company follows in the footsteps of Mercor and Scale AI, both of which have built billion-dollar businesses around human data work. But AfterQuery's focus on replicating professional workflows, not just labeling data, positions it as a specialized player in the growing 'human-in-the-loop' AI sector, where experts remain essential to advanced model quality.
report.impact: AfterQuery's rapid ascent signals that the AI industry's bottleneck is shifting from raw compute to high-quality, domain-specific training data. For model developers, this means expert human labor is becoming a premium, scarce resource — and startups that can efficiently organize such talent will capture significant value. For regular users, the payoff will eventually be AI agents that don't just answer questions but actually perform professional work, like drafting legal documents, diagnosing medical cases, or planning complex financial strategies. However, the valuation also raises questions: with record speed and high ARR, there's pressure to grow sustainably. If AfterQuery can maintain its edge, it may accelerate a broader trend where AI quality depends less on algorithm breakthroughs and more on the real-world expertise embedded in training data.
report.tools: For readers tracking this space, watch AfterQuery's competitors Mercor and Scale AI for market benchmarks. On the open-source side, explore Label Studio and Argilla for human-in-the-loop annotation workflows, and Cleanlab for automated data-quality correction. These tools help teams build and manage professional-quality training datasets, especially when combining expert feedback with model iteration.
